title: Monetary Policy
welcome_lead: Central banks steer the economy by adjusting interest rates and money supply.
meta_desc: A-Level Macroeconomics: monetary policy and transmission.
final_note: Monetary policy is powerful but slow - and unevenly distributed.

walkthroughs.body_html: The main tool is the bank rate; in crisis the bank also uses QE and forward guidance. Higher rates slow borrowing and spending; lower rates do the reverse.
Rate changes feed through borrowing costs, asset prices, exchange rates and expectations. Effects take 12 to 24 months - policy must be set looking ahead.
In a liquidity trap, very low rates do not boost borrowing because confidence is too low. Japan in the 1990s and Europe after 2008 both struggled to escape.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between monetary and fiscal policy?
options: Monetary policy is about money and fiscal policy is about taxes.
Monetary policy uses interest rates and money supply controlled by the central bank; fiscal policy uses government taxation and spending controlled by the Treasury.
Both terms mean the same thing — government economic policy.
QE is when banks charge negative interest on deposits.

mcqs.q: How does quantitative easing actually work?
options: Both terms mean the same thing — government economic policy.
QE is the central bank printing money and handing it to citizens.

The central bank creates reserves to buy financial assets (mostly government bonds) from banks and pension funds, raising asset prices and lowering yields — stimulating spending and lending indirectly. It is not literally printing physical cash for the public.
QE is when banks charge negative interest on deposits.

mcqs.q: How does raising interest rates reduce inflation?
options: Higher rates make borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive, reducing consumption and investment — lowering aggregate demand and slowing price rises.
Higher interest rates make money more valuable so inflation falls automatically.
Both terms mean the same thing — government economic policy.
Higher interest rates directly force shops to lower their prices.
